fr-01.titre_court: Algorithmic video surveillance, 2024 Olympic Games law
fr-01.phrase: The law of May 19, 2023 on the 2024 Games authorized, on an experimental basis, the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images, originally until March 31, 2025. This experiment was then renewed by laws passed in 2026.
fr-01.limite: The March 2025 end date was replaced by a renewal until 2027, then 2030: it is no longer the current state.
fr-01.experimentation: initial end date March 31, 2025; renewed until December 31, 2027, then December 31, 2030
fr-01.levier_mots: « a autorisé, à titre expérimental, le traitement algorithmique des images de vidéoprotection »

w10.mecanisme: The text authorizes, on an experimental basis, the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images to detect and report certain events, originally until March 31, 2025.
w10.limite: That end date has passed and the experiment was then renewed (“Law of March 20, 2026: renewal of the experiment”, then “Law of August 18, 2026: experiment, 2030 end date”); the facts come from the Constitutional Council decision and the CNIL fact sheet, as the text of the law itself was not read.

fr-01.verification: The text of the law was read in the Senate's "petite loi" (senat.fr/petite-loi-ameli/2022-2023/497.html), not on Légifrance.

fr-02.titre_court: Decision of May 17, 2023: 2024 Olympic Games law
fr-02.phrase: The Constitutional Council ruled Article 10 of the 2024 Olympic Games law constitutional, with one reservation: the prefect must immediately end an authorization whose conditions are no longer met.
fr-02.limite: Validates the 2023 experiment only; says nothing about the later renewals, which have their own decisions. Article 7 of the law is struck down as a legislative rider (cavalier législatif), unrelated to AI.
fr-02.experimentation: March 31, 2025 (end date set by the law under review, §47)
fr-02.levier_mots: « le préfet doit mettre fin immédiatement à une autorisation dont les conditions ne sont plus réunies »

w10.mecanisme: The decision rules Article 10 constitutional with one reservation: the prefect must immediately end an authorization whose conditions are no longer met.
w10.limite: The same decision declares the article constitutional, so it lets the tool exist, and it applies only to the 2023 experiment, not to the renewals.

fr-03.titre_court: Law of March 20, 2026: renewal of the experiment
fr-03.phrase: The law of March 20, 2026 renewed until December 31, 2027 the experiment in algorithmic image processing provided for by the 2023 law. The Constitutional Council ruled these dates constitutional.
fr-03.limite: The Council dismisses the privacy objections by saying that these provisions do not affect privacy « par elles-mêmes » (§180); it does not say that the tool carries no risk. The 2027 date is later replaced by 2030: it is no longer the current date.
fr-03.experimentation: December 31, 2027 (renewal under Article 47 of this law), later extended to December 31, 2030; evaluation report due no later than September 30, 2027
fr-03.levier_mots: « a reconduit jusqu'au 31 décembre 2027 l'expérimentation du traitement algorithmique d'images »

w10.mecanisme: The law renews until December 31, 2027 the experiment in algorithmic image processing provided for by the 2023 law, and the Council rules these dates constitutional.
w10.limite: The Council dismisses the privacy objections by saying that these provisions do not affect privacy « par elles-mêmes » (§180), and the 2027 date is later replaced by 2030 (“Law of August 18, 2026: experiment, 2030 end date”).

fr-04.titre_court: Law of August 18, 2026: experiment, 2030 end date
fr-04.phrase: The law of August 18, 2026 postpones to December 31, 2030 the end of the experiment in algorithmic image processing and extends it to certain buildings and places open to the public that are exposed to a risk of terrorism or of serious harm to people. The Constitutional Council ruled these provisions constitutional, with one reservation: for places exposed to a permanent risk, the authorization cannot exceed three months.
fr-04.limite: The law contains other articles, several of them struck down (Article 10 of the law referred, administrative closure, etc.): this entry says nothing about them. §541 describes the regime (neither facial recognition nor biometric data); it does not prohibit all future use. The name « Ripost » appears neither on the Senate page nor in the decision.
fr-04.levier_mots: « reporte au 31 décembre 2030 le terme de l'expérimentation » ; « l'autorisation ne peut excéder trois mois »

w10:frein.mecanisme: The Constitutional Council sets a reservation: for places exposed to a permanent risk, the authorization cannot exceed three months.
w10:frein.limite: The reservation covers only processing in buildings and places exposed to a permanent risk (§544); for exceptional circumstances, the law already caps it at three months (§542).

w10:vers.mecanisme: The law postpones to December 31, 2030 the end date of the experiment on algorithmic processing of images and extends it to certain buildings and places open to the public exposed to a risk of terrorism or serious harm to persons.
w10:vers.limite: The Council finds these provisions compliant and describes a regime without facial recognition or biometric data (§541), which does not rule out every future use; the other articles of the law, several of which were struck down, are not covered.

fr-05.phrase: A bill filed in the Senate on May 12, 2026 aims to make algorithmic video surveillance general; the Senate page shows neither a committee report nor a vote.
fr-05.limite: Filing a bill is not adopting it. The text sets no end date for an experiment: it creates a permanent regime (authorization by decree after an opinion from the CNIL, then by the prefect). Nowhere does the text say that it « reprend le régime des JO ».
fr-05.levier_mots: « vise à généraliser la vidéoprotection algorithmique »

w10.mecanisme: The text proposes that images from authorized video surveillance systems may be subject to processing that includes an artificial intelligence system.
w10.limite: Filing a bill is not adopting it, and the Senate page shows neither a committee report nor a vote; the text creates a permanent regime with no experimental end date, and nowhere does it say that it takes over the Games regime.

fr-06.phrase: A bill filed in the Senate on December 12, 2025 proposes to authorize the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images in public transport.
fr-06.limite: Filing a bill is not adopting it.
fr-06.levier_mots: « propose d'autoriser le traitement algorithmique des images de vidéoprotection dans les transports en commun »

w10.mecanisme: The text proposes to authorize the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images in public transport.
w10.limite: Filing a bill is not adopting it, and the tracking page, dated June 19, 2026, shows no step after filing without establishing that no review has taken place since.

fr-06.verification: The tracking page shows no step after filing and was last updated on June 19, 2026: it does not establish that no review took place after that date.

fr-07.phrase: On February 16, 2026, the National Assembly adopted at first reading a text authorizing, on an experimental basis until December 31, 2027, the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images in certain shops to prevent theft. The text was sent to the Senate (No. 402) and is not a law.
fr-07.limite: Text not adopted by the Senate as of the date of the tracking page (updated August 24, 2026); it has the force of law nowhere. Does not say that shops already deploy these tools.
fr-07.experimentation: December 31, 2027 (evaluation report due no later than September 30, 2027)
fr-07.levier_mots: « autorisant à titre expérimental, jusqu'au 31 décembre 2027, le traitement algorithmique des images de vidéoprotection dans certains commerces pour prévenir le vol »

w10.mecanisme: The text proposes to authorize, on an experimental basis until December 31, 2027, the algorithmic processing of video surveillance images in certain shops, for the sole purpose of preventing theft.
w10.limite: Adopted at first reading by the National Assembly and sent to the Senate (No. 402), it is not a law; the actors concerned are shopkeepers, not a state authority, and the text does not say that shops already deploy these tools.

fr-08.titre_court: Decision of April 24, 2025: security in public transport
fr-08.phrase: On April 24, 2025, the Constitutional Council struck down, on procedural grounds (legislative rider), the extension until March 1, 2027 of the algorithmic video surveillance experiment that had been slipped into the law on security in public transport.
fr-08.limite: A PROCEDURAL censure, not a ruling on the merits of algorithmic video surveillance (VSA): the Council writes that it rules « sans qu’il soit besoin de se prononcer sur les autres griefs » (§138). It does not allow one to say that the Council finds VSA unconstitutional.
fr-08.experimentation: extension until March 1, 2027 struck down (legislative rider)
fr-08.levier_mots: « a censuré, pour vice de procédure (cavalier législatif), la prolongation jusqu'au 1er mars 2027 de l'expérimentation »

w10.mecanisme: The Constitutional Council strikes down, on procedural grounds, the extension until March 1, 2027 of the algorithmic video surveillance experiment added to the law on security in public transport.
w10.limite: It is a procedural censure (legislative rider), not a ruling on the merits: the Council rules « sans qu’il soit besoin de se prononcer sur les autres griefs » (§138).

fr-09.phrase: The law of June 13, 2025 on drug trafficking was promulgated after a decision of the Constitutional Council finding it partly constitutional.
fr-09.limite: A single text, many measures; says nothing about encryption in its final version.
fr-09.raison_sans_levier: All that is known is that the law was promulgated after a decision finding it partly constitutional; nothing is established about its content.
fr-09.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. All that is known is that the law was promulgated after a decision of the Constitutional Council finding it partly constitutional, nothing about its content; the censure that matters here is the one described in “Decision of June 12, 2025: drug trafficking law”.

fr-10.titre_court: Decision of June 12, 2025: drug trafficking law
fr-10.phrase: On June 12, 2025, the Constitutional Council struck down Article 15 of the drug trafficking law, which extended the intelligence technique known as the algorithm to the prevention of organized crime and delinquency, as well as the use of full internet addresses in this technique.
fr-10.limite: No passage on decrypting messaging services: the decision contains no occurrence of « chiffr » or « messagerie ». Lawmakers returned to the subject in 2026.
fr-10.levier_mots: « a censuré l'article 15 de la loi narcotrafic »

w10.mecanisme: The Constitutional Council strikes down Article 15 of the drug trafficking law, which extended the intelligence technique known as the algorithm to the prevention of organized crime and delinquency, as well as the use of full internet addresses in this technique.
w10.limite: The decision says nothing about encryption (no occurrence of « chiffr » or « messagerie »), and a 2026 law rewrites the technique, extending it again, and is ruled constitutional (“Law of August 16, 2026: the algorithm technique”).

fr-11.titre_court: Article 8 ter: access to intelligible content
fr-11.phrase: On February 4, 2025, the Senate adopted an Article 8 ter amending the Internal Security Code (code de la sécurité intérieure) to require taking the technical measures that allow access to the intelligible content of data collected under an intelligence authorization. The National Assembly deleted it on April 1, 2025, and the joint committee text (commission mixte paritaire) adopted by the Senate on April 28, 2025 lists it as deleted.
fr-11.limite: The Senate text does not mention messaging services (the word « déchiffrement » appears only in the words it deletes): it amends Article L. 871-1 (cryptology services) and creates an Article L. 34-18 in the Postal and Electronic Communications Code (code des postes et communications électroniques). The article was deleted.
fr-11.levier_mots: « imposer de prendre les mesures techniques permettant l'accès au contenu intelligible de données collectées sous autorisation de renseignement »

w10.mecanisme: The text adopted by the Senate proposes to require taking the technical measures that allow access to the intelligible content of data collected under an intelligence authorization.
w10.limite: The National Assembly deleted it on April 1, 2025 and it does not appear in the law of June 13, 2025; the text does not mention messaging services, it amends Article L. 871-1 and creates an Article L. 34-18 of the Postal and Electronic Communications Code (code des postes et communications électroniques).

fr-12.phrase: In May 2026, the parliamentary intelligence delegation (délégation parlementaire au renseignement) wrote that targeted access by the intelligence services and the courts to encrypted messaging services is, in its view, legitimate and necessary.
fr-12.limite: An advisory position of a parliamentary delegation: it creates no power and is not a law.
fr-12.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It is the position of a parliamentary delegation; its detailed recommendations were not checked in full, so one cannot say that it proposes anything.
fr-12.levier_mots: « un accès ciblé des services de renseignement et de la justice aux messageries chiffrées est, selon elle, légitime et nécessaire » (a position, no power created)
fr-12.verification: Pages 4 onward (detailed recommendations) were not checked in full. The exact date of May 4, 2026 does not appear in the DPR's own PDF: it is given by the opinion of the Senate's law committee ("Communication de la délégation parlementaire au renseignement, 4 mai 2026").

fr-13.titre_court: Resilience bill: deletion of Article 16 bis
fr-13.phrase: On November 10, 2026, the National Assembly voted, by 69 votes to 37 (one abstention), to delete Article 16 bis of the resilience bill, which the Senate had added and which prohibited requiring encryption providers to install mechanisms that deliberately weaken security. The bill has not yet been adopted.
fr-13.limite: The bill is not adopted; a joint committee (commission mixte paritaire) may or may not restore the article. The text of Article 16 bis protected encryption: the Assembly removed a safeguard that the Senate had written.
fr-13.levier_mots: « la suppression de l'article 16 bis du projet de loi résilience » (removes a safeguard, creates no access)

w10.mecanisme: The resilience bill loses its Article 16 bis, deleted by the National Assembly by 69 votes to 37, an article that prohibited requiring encryption providers to install mechanisms that deliberately weaken security.
w10.limite: The bill is not adopted and a joint committee may or may not restore the article; the Assembly did not weaken encryption, it removed a safeguard written by the Senate, and this link does not say that the bill creates a power of access.

fr-13.verification: The final vote on the whole bill announced by the press for November 17 is not confirmed by the National Assembly's file page. Senate page frozen as of March 17, 2026.

fr-14.titre_court: Law of August 16, 2026: the algorithm technique
fr-14.phrase: The law of August 16, 2026 on military programming rewrites the intelligence technique known as the algorithm: it extends it to the prevention of organized crime and delinquency and allows the use of certain full internet addresses. The Constitutional Council ruled these provisions constitutional on August 6, 2026.
fr-14.limite: The Constitutional Council rules the provisions constitutional by relying on safeguards (opinion of the CNCTR, review by the Council of State (Conseil d'État), internet addresses limited to specific cases, §52). Does not say how many people are affected.
fr-14.levier_mots: « l'étend à la prévention de la criminalité et de la délinquance organisées et permet d'utiliser certaines adresses internet complètes »

w10.mecanisme: In its Article 32, the law rewrites the intelligence technique known as the algorithm: it extends it to the prevention of organized crime and delinquency and allows the use of certain full internet addresses.
w10.limite: The Council rules these provisions constitutional by relying on safeguards (opinion of the CNCTR, review by the Council of State, addresses limited to specific cases, §52) without saying how many people are affected; the July 1, 2029 limit comes from the opinion on the bill as filed and was not checked again in the promulgated law.

fr-14.verification: The time limit (July 1, 2029) comes from the Senate's opinion on the bill as filed: the promulgated law was not read on this point.

fr-15.titre_court: Intelligence technique known as the algorithm
fr-15.phrase: The algorithm technique, introduced on an experimental basis in 2015, was made permanent in 2021; it automatically processes connection data to detect weak signals of threats. It was rewritten by the law of August 16, 2026.
fr-15.limite: The purposes cited are those in force before the law of August 16, 2026. Does not say how many people are affected. The CNCTR's sentence ("ni une surveillance de masse ni un automatisme") is a quoted claim, not an established fact.
fr-15.experimentation: national defense and foreign interference purposes: until July 1, 2028 according to the Senate opinion of May 2026, before the law of August 16, 2026
fr-15.levier_mots: « traite automatiquement des données de connexion pour détecter des signaux faibles de menaces »

w10.mecanisme: The intelligence technique known as the algorithm, introduced on an experimental basis in 2015 and made permanent in 2021, automatically processes connection data to detect weak signals of threats.
w10.limite: The verified sources do not say how many people are affected, and the CNCTR's sentence (« ni une surveillance de masse ni un automatisme ») is a quoted claim, not an established fact; the source is the opinion of a Senate committee and the article is rewritten by “Law of August 16, 2026: the algorithm technique”.

fr-15.verification: Source of the quotation: the opinion of a Senate committee (May 2026), not the text of the laws; the numbers of the 2015 and 2021 laws were not read.

fr-16.phrase: On May 20, 2021, the Constitutional Council struck down Article 48 of the law on global security (on-board cameras) and part of Article 47 (cameras mounted on drones).
fr-16.limite: Partial censure: Article 47 is not struck down in full. The law was promulgated on May 25, 2021 after the decision, with other articles struck down (1, 2 I, 41, 52 I, 26, 57, 63, 68, 69).
fr-16.levier_mots: « a censuré l'article 48 [...] (caméras embarquées) et une grande partie de l'article 47 (caméras installées sur des drones) »

w10.mecanisme: The Constitutional Council strikes down Article 48 of the law on global security (on-board cameras) and a large part of Article 47 (cameras mounted on drones).
w10.limite: The censure is partial, since Article 47 is not struck down in full, and the legal framework for drones after 2021 was not checked.

fr-16.verification: The legal framework for drones after 2021 was not checked here.

fr-17.titre_court: Law of May 21, 2024: securing and regulating the digital space (SREN)
fr-17.phrase: The SREN law of May 21, 2024 was promulgated after a partial censure by the Constitutional Council, which upheld Arcom's role in setting a standard for age verification on pornographic websites.
fr-17.limite: The censured Article 10 set the goal of 100% of French people having a free digital identity by January 1, 2027: it is struck down as a legislative rider (§58-59), not on the merits. Article 19 (online contempt) is struck down on the merits (freedom of expression). Arcom's standard concerns minors' access to pornography, not social networks.
fr-17.raison_sans_levier: It concerns an age standard for pornography.
fr-17.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It concerns age and minors' access to pornography; no world in the game deals with this subject.

fr-18.phrase: The law of July 7, 2023 on digital majority provides that social networks refuse registration to under-15s without parental authorization, but it has not entered into force: according to a review by the National Assembly's cultural affairs committee dated February 3, 2026, none of the required regulatory measures has been adopted.
fr-18.limite: The incompatibility with European law (Breton letter of August 14, 2023) is asserted by this National Assembly report, not checked in the letter itself.
fr-18.raison_sans_levier: It concerns the digital majority on social networks, and its application is not established.
fr-18.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It concerns age and minors' access to social networks; no world in the game deals with this subject.
fr-18.verification: Status established as of February 3, 2026 (National Assembly, CACE communication), not as of November 14, 2026: no implementing decree found since, but not having found one does not show that none exists.

fr-19.titre_court: Law of August 24, 2026: minors, social networks
fr-19.phrase: On August 14, 2026, the Constitutional Council declared unconstitutional Article 1 of the law aimed at protecting minors from the risks to which the use of social networks exposes them, which prohibited under-fifteens from accessing certain online services. The law was promulgated on August 24, 2026 without this article.
fr-19.limite: Censure of this article only: the Council "ne s'est pas prononcé" on the other provisions (§23). It censures the lack of legal safeguards.
fr-19.raison_sans_levier: It concerns minors' access to social networks.
fr-19.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It concerns age and minors' access to social networks; no world in the game deals with this subject.
fr-19.verification: The content of the other articles of the promulgated law was not checked here.

fr-20.titre_court: Notification of September 14, 2026: minors and social networks
fr-20.phrase: On September 14, 2026, the President of the Republic wrote on X, according to Brut (with AFP) and Siècle Digital, that the government was notifying the European Commission of new wording of the text on minors' access to social networks, one month after the Constitutional Council's decision.
fr-20.limite: No bill filed in Parliament, no official text read: it is an announcement, reported by the press. The content of the text (a list of features deemed harmful, parental exemptions from 13 to 15) comes from an anonymous source cited by Le Figaro: it is not established. The target end date (spring) is a hope of the President, not a legal timetable.
fr-20.raison_sans_levier: It is the announcement of the notification of a text on minors' access.
fr-20.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It is the announcement of a text on age and minors' access to social networks; no world in the game deals with this subject.

fr-21.titre_court: Darmanin, TF1: facial recognition and the criminal records processing file (TAJ)
fr-21.phrase: On October 19, 2026, on TF1's 8 p.m. news, Minister of Justice (garde des Sceaux) Gérald Darmanin announced that he wanted to use facial recognition to compare images of violence posted on social networks with the photos in the TAJ file.
fr-21.limite: A statement is not a legal text; no text puts it into effect.
fr-21.levier_mots: « a annoncé vouloir recourir à la reconnaissance faciale pour comparer des images de violences [...] aux photos du fichier TAJ »

w10.mecanisme: The statement announces the intention to use facial recognition to compare images of violence posted on social networks with the photos in the TAJ file.
w10.limite: A statement is not a legal text and no text puts it into effect; the full sentence is carried by only one outlet and is not quoted, only two fragments being established by two outlets.

fr-21.verification: The full sentence "on va utiliser le moyen de la reconnaissance faciale sur le TAJ..." is carried word for word only by Next (transcript). The other two outlets confirm the announcement and two exact fragments that fit into it. TF1 video not opened.

fr-22.titre_court: Darmanin, post on X: facial recognition
fr-22.phrase: According to an AFP dispatch of May 23, 2025, picked up by Phonandroid on May 27, 2025, Minister of Justice (garde des Sceaux) Gérald Darmanin had written on his X account that « utiliser la technologie et la reconnaissance faciale, ce sont les solutions pour lutter drastiquement contre l'insécurité ».
fr-22.limite: A statement is not a law. The working group of May 23, 2025 comes from his entourage, not from him.
fr-22.date_stade: before May 23, 2025 (date of the AFP dispatch; date of the post not established)
fr-22.levier_mots: « utiliser la technologie et la reconnaissance faciale, ce sont les solutions pour lutter drastiquement contre l'insécurité »

w10.mecanisme: The statement posted on X says that facial recognition is, along with technology, one of the solutions against insecurity.
w10.limite: It is a general statement that describes no mechanism, and only this sentence is established by two outlets, the other sentences reported from May 2025 not being picked up.

fr-22.verification: Only the X sentence is confirmed by two separate outlets; the post itself was not opened. The sentence "à Dubaï, il y a la reconnaissance faciale" (interview of May 5) rests on only ONE AFP dispatch (Banque des Territoires and Boursorama reproduce it identically).

fr-23.phrase: A member of the National Assembly questioned the Minister of the Interior in a written question published on May 12, 2026 about an alleged use of facial recognition software linked to the TAJ file; the page showed no answer.
fr-23.limite: An allegation taken up by a member of parliament, based on an investigation by the outlet Disclose: not an established fact. The claim of a "manifestement illégal" use is the member's.
fr-23.raison_sans_levier: It is a member of parliament's question about an alleged use: it neither creates nor limits anything.
fr-23.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. It is a member of parliament's written question about an alleged use: it neither proposes nor limits anything.
fr-23.verification: The consultation figures (375,000 in 2019, nearly 2.5 million in 2024) are those of the question, not verified.

fr-24.titre_court: CNIL: formal notices, video analysis software
fr-24.phrase: In December 2024, the CNIL announced that it had issued formal notices to the Ministry of the Interior and six municipalities concerning video analysis software, including a facial recognition function added to the BriefCam software.
fr-24.limite: A formal notice is not a sanction; the CNIL found no facial recognition in the municipalities it inspected. For the ministry, it found one isolated case of use of the facial recognition function.
fr-24.levier_mots: « a mis en demeure le ministère de l'Intérieur et six communes »

w10.mecanisme: The CNIL issues formal notices to the Ministry of the Interior and six municipalities concerning video analysis software, including a facial recognition function added to the BriefCam software.
w10.limite: A formal notice is not a sanction, the CNIL found no facial recognition in the municipalities it inspected and found only one isolated case for the ministry.

fr-24.verification: The follow-up (closure or sanction) was not opened.

fr-25.phrase: On June 12, 2023, the Senate adopted a bill that prohibits in principle remote biometric identification in public spaces, except with consent, with experimental exceptions for three years; the text awaits review by the National Assembly.
fr-25.limite: A text not definitively adopted, adopted by the Senate only.
fr-25.experimentation: 3 years from promulgation for the derogating provisions (Article 1 bis)
fr-25.levier_mots: « interdit en principe l'identification biométrique à distance dans l'espace public »

w10.mecanisme: The text adopted by the Senate proposes to prohibit in principle remote biometric identification in public spaces, except with consent, with experimental exceptions for three years.
w10.limite: Adopted by the Senate only, it awaits review by the National Assembly, the tracking page dates from January 30, 2025 and the status since then is not established.

fr-25.verification: Senate tracking page updated on January 30, 2025; the National Assembly file shows no review either: the status since then is not established. The 2023 text was read for the prohibition in principle and the experiment, not for the detailed list of purposes.

fr-26.phrase: A bill filed in the National Assembly on October 14, 2025 provides for a social contribution on automated systems that compete with salaried work.
fr-26.limite: This is not a universal basic income. Filing a bill is not adopting it: the tracking page shows only the filing and the referral to committee. The text provides for an experiment starting January 1, 2026, a date already past when it was filed.
fr-26.experimentation: text: experimental phase from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2027, general entry into force on January 1, 2028
fr-26.sans_lien: The game links it to no world. The proposed contribution is not a universal basic income, and no verified text concerns the abolition of property. It is filed under the “Distributing wealth” lever.
fr-26.levier_mots: « prévoit une contribution sociale sur les systèmes automatisés qui concurrencent le travail salarié » (« ce n'est pas un revenu universel »)
fr-26.verification: The OECD figure (16.4% of jobs) is a claim made by the authors in the explanatory memorandum, not verified here.

ue-01.phrase: According to the latest official document read (Council presidency document of September 30, 2026), the European regulation against online child sexual abuse is under negotiation between Parliament and the Council. At the sixth trilogue (Sept. 29, 2026), no breakthrough was reached on searches and detection in non-public content; an agreement in principle, tied to the whole package, would limit detection orders in public content to already known content. The seventh trilogue is provisionally scheduled for December 2026.
ue-01.limite: The Council document (WK 15082/2026, dated Sept. 30, 2026, marked LIMITE) reports negotiating positions, not an agreed text. The exclusion of end-to-end encrypted content is the Council presidency's position on an article that is still open (Article Z), not an adopted rule. The text does not make it possible to say that scanning of messaging services will be imposed, or that it will be ruled out. The Council says it has no mandate for detection orders in private content. For this content, Parliament wants orders targeted at specific users, limited to known content, as a last resort. "Chat Control" is a press name, not an official title.
ue-01.levier_mots: « ordres de détection » ; « limiterait les ordres de détection en contenu public aux contenus déjà connus »

w10:frein.mecanisme: An agreement in principle, tied to the whole package, would limit detection orders in public content to already known content.
w10:frein.limite: This is a negotiating position on a package that has not been agreed, with the Council saying it has no mandate for detection orders in private content.

w10:vers.mecanisme: The regulation under negotiation provides for detection orders, and at the sixth trilogue no breakthrough was reached on searches and detection in non-public content.
w10:vers.limite: The Council document reports negotiating positions, not an agreed text: it does not allow saying that scanning of messaging will be imposed, nor that it will be dropped (“Chat Control” is a press name).

ue-02.phrase: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881, published in the Official Journal on July 28, 2026 and in force since July 31, 2026, allows messaging service providers to use technologies to detect child sexual abuse, until April 3, 2028. Its Article 1 excludes communications protected by end-to-end encryption.
ue-02.limite: The text allows detection by providers (a derogation regime, with no obligation read in Article 1); it does not impose scanning. It is temporary and does not settle the substantive regulation. It does not say what providers do in practice. ue-04.titre_court: European AI regulation (AI Act): general framework

ue-05.titre_court: European AI regulation (AI Act), Article 5: biometric identification
ue-05.phrase: Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits the use by law enforcement of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces, unless it is strictly necessary for one of three objectives: searching for victims or missing persons, preventing a specific and imminent threat, locating or identifying a suspect of a serious offense. Each use requires prior authorization from a judicial or independent authority, with an urgency exception (request within 24 hours).
ue-05.limite: The text targets real-time use; it does not say that delayed identification is prohibited. Article 5, paragraph 5, leaves each State to decide whether or not to authorize this use and to set its rules in national law: the regulation therefore does not say that a State practices it. Article 2, paragraph 3, excludes uses exclusively for national security. A brake and an open door at the same time, depending on the reading.
ue-05.nature: provision of a regulation (prohibition with exceptions)
ue-05.application: February 2, 2025 for Article 5 (Chapter II). Points (ba), (bb) and paragraphs 1a and 1b, added by 2026/1744, apply from December 2, 2026 and do not concern biometric identification.

ue-08.limite: The official OEIL label is "Awaiting committee decision"; the date of July 27, 2026 is that of the latest documents tabled, not of a decision. The precise content of the proposal (definition of personal data, model training) is not summarized here. The text is not adopted.

ue-09.phrase: The GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, has applied since May 25, 2018. Its Article 22 gives every person the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them; Article 9 prohibits in principle the processing of biometric data intended to uniquely identify a person.
ue-09.limite: Paragraphs 2 to 4 of Article 22 and paragraph 2 of Article 9 provide for exceptions (contract, Union or Member State law, explicit consent): the right is therefore not absolute. The text read is the version published in the OJ in 2016; an amendment under way is not adopted. The GDPR does not say what police facial recognition is: that falls under other texts (Police Directive, AI Act).
ue-09.nature: regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council
ue-09.entree_en_vigueur: May 24, 2016 (twentieth day after the OJ of May 4, 2016)

ue-13.phrase: Regulation (EU) 2024/1083 on media freedom, generally applicable since August 8, 2025, requires States to protect journalists' sources and their confidential communications. int-01.phrase: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI was opened for signature on September 5, 2024, in Vilnius. The European Union ratified it on May 15, 2026. int-07.titre_court: Court of Justice of the EU: data retention
int-07.phrase: On October 6, 2020, the Court of Justice of the EU ruled that Union law precludes national legislation providing, as a preventive measure, for the general and indiscriminate retention of traffic and location data. It allows exceptions, in particular in the event of a serious threat to national security that is genuine and present or foreseeable, subject to effective review.

The judgment concerns Directive 2002/58, not a European bill.

chf-01.libelle_court: AI researchers: median chance of extinction or permanent and severe disempowerment
chf-01.phrase: In 2023, a survey of AI researchers (AI Impacts) asked about human extinction; the median answer was 5%.
chf-01.limite: A median of expert judgments is neither a measured chance nor an established risk. Mean 16.2% versus median 5% (high tail). Participation rate 15%. Each question was asked only of a randomly drawn subset: sample size 1,321, not 2,778.
chf-01.population: Researchers who published in 2022 in one of six venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, JMLR), 2,778 respondents out of 18,459 valid addresses, response rate 15%

chf-02.phrase: According to this 2023 survey, between 38% and 51% of the researchers surveyed gave at least a 10% chance to an outcome on the scale of an extinction, depending on how the question was worded.
chf-02.limite: Share of people who gave a chance, not the chance of extinction. The range comes from the wording, and each bar has its own sample size. The text on p. 14 says 41.2 to 51.4 (without the impact question), the summary says 37.8 to 51.4.
chf-02.population: Researchers who published in 2022 in one of six venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, JMLR), 2,778 respondents out of 18,459 valid addresses, response rate 15%

chf-04.libelle_court: AI researchers judging good outcomes more likely than bad ones
chf-04.phrase: In the same survey, 68% of researchers judged good outcomes more likely than bad ones; 58% also judged an extremely bad outcome non-negligible.
chf-04.limite: The two proportions overlap: among those who judge good outcomes more likely than bad ones, 48.4% give at least a 5% chance to an extremely bad outcome; in addition, 64% give a non-zero chance to both extremes. They therefore do not form two distinct camps.
chf-04.population: Researchers who published in 2022 in one of six venues (NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, AAAI, IJCAI, JMLR), 2,778 respondents out of 18,459 valid addresses, response rate 15%
chf-04.effectif: n=2,704 (caption of figure 11, 2023; the link to the 68.3% is not written word for word in the text)
chf-04.unite: % judging good outcomes more likely than bad ones; 57.8% judge an extremely bad outcome non-negligible (>= 5%)

chf-05.libelle_court: US adults: superhuman AI never developed, or only once controllable and safe
chf-05.phrase: In a US poll from September-October 2025, 30% of adults said that a superhuman AI should never be developed and 34% only once it is shown to be controllable and safe.
chf-05.limite: Opinion of US adults after reading a description (the respondent read 'There is controversy as to whether Superhuman AI should be developed', PDF page 20). Sponsor = an organization that advocates a position on the subject. Margin of error +/- 2.2 points at 95% (page 4), larger on subsamples. US adults, not France or Europe. Another 64% appears in this report, for another question. Total of the six superhuman AI response options = 101 (rounding). This total adds two answers: 30% and 34%. For expert-level AI, the total adds 17% and 40%, i.e. 57%.
chf-05.population: Adults residing in the United States, sample weighted to the national population, online interviews by SMS and panel, random selection
chf-05.auteur: Bryson Gillette Insights for the Future of Life Institute, « Opinions on Advanced AI Development: Findings from a National Survey of Adults »

chf-06.libelle_court: US adults supporting an international treaty banning superhuman AI
chf-06.phrase: In a US poll from September-October 2025, 57% of adults supported an international treaty banning superhuman AI, 17% opposed it.
chf-06.limite: Declared opinion of US adults. Sponsor = an organization that advocates a position on the subject. Margin of error +/- 2.2 points at 95% (page 4), larger on subsamples. US adults, not France or Europe. The item is one of eight; the introductory wording is not published (only the item label is known). Establishes neither the feasibility nor the existence of such a treaty. Support adds two answers: 36% strongly and 20% somewhat, i.e. 56% based on the chart's rounded values; the report prints 57%. 17% of the adults surveyed oppose it.
chf-06.population: Adults residing in the United States, sample weighted to the national population, online interviews by SMS and panel, random selection
chf-06.auteur: Bryson Gillette Insights for the Future of Life Institute, « Opinions on Advanced AI Development: Findings from a National Survey of Adults »

chf-07.libelle_court: US adults: immediate pause on AI until its safety is demonstrated
chf-07.phrase: In a US poll from September-October 2025, 64% of adults supported an immediate pause in the development of advanced AI until its safety is demonstrated.
chf-07.limite: Sponsor = an organization that advocates a position on the subject. Margin of error +/- 2.2 points at 95% (page 4), larger on subsamples. US adults, not France or Europe. Another 64% exists in this report: the sum of two response options of another question. For comparison, in the same list: 'Slow, heavily regulated development' 73% support, 'Unrestricted development' 25% support and 55% opposition. Support adds two answers: 39% strongly and 24% somewhat, i.e. 63% based on the chart's rounded values; the report prints 64%. 18% of the adults surveyed oppose it.
chf-07.population: Adults residing in the United States, sample weighted to the national population, online interviews by SMS and panel, random selection
chf-07.auteur: Bryson Gillette Insights for the Future of Life Institute, « Opinions on Advanced AI Development: Findings from a National Survey of Adults »

chf-08.libelle_court: French people opposed to being recognized and identified without their knowledge
chf-08.phrase: In January 2022, 63% of the French people surveyed by the Défenseur des droits (French rights ombudsman) were opposed to being recognized and identified without their knowledge.
chf-08.limite: An opinion in principle on a use described in one sentence, not on a real system or a specific use (police, event). Poll from January 2022, before the 2024 Olympics law and the AI Act. Percentages of the total, non-responses included (~1%). Pages cited = printed numbers (PDF page minus 1).
chf-08.population: 2,016 people representative of French people aged 18 and over, quota method (sex, age, socio-professional category, region, size of urban area), online
chf-08.question_tr: Would you yourself be in favor of or opposed to the use of technologies to… [item] Recognize and identify you without your knowledge (in %); response options: Very much in favor / Somewhat in favor / Somewhat opposed / Strongly opposed / No answer
chf-08.auteur: Défenseur des droits (Defender of Rights, France), « Perception du développement des technologies biométriques en France : entre manque d’information et demande d’encadrement »

chf-09.libelle_court: French people: views on everyday deployment of biometric technologies in public
chf-09.phrase: In January 2022, the French people surveyed were split almost evenly on an everyday deployment of biometric technologies in public space: 48% in favor, 51% opposed (sums calculated by us).
chf-09.limite: No total is printed; the text on p. 12 says only 'plutôt opposés à une utilisation systématique et quotidienne'. A narrow split, uncertainty interval not published. "Biometric technologies" groups together authentication, identification and assessment. Poll from January 2022, before the 2024 Olympics law and the AI Act. Percentages of the total, non-responses included (~1%). Pages cited = printed numbers (PDF page minus 1).
chf-09.population: 2,016 people representative of French people aged 18 and over, quota method (sex, age, socio-professional category, region, size of urban area), online
chf-09.question_tr: Would you be in favor of or opposed to France deploying and using biometric technologies in streets and public spaces on an everyday basis? (in %)
chf-09.auteur: Défenseur des droits (Defender of Rights, France), « Perception du développement des technologies biométriques en France : entre manque d’information et demande d’encadrement »
chf-09.unite: % (16 + 32; 30 + 21), sums calculated by us; no answer 1%

chf-12.libelle_court: French people judging it important or a priority to better regulate biometrics
chf-12.phrase: In January 2022, 84% of the French people surveyed judged it important, or even an absolute priority (47%), to strengthen the legal framework for biometric technologies to better guarantee people's rights.
chf-12.limite: Measures a declared priority, not a belief about the effectiveness of a framework. Does not say which framework. Same chart: ban in certain areas 32% priority + 39% important = 71%; suspend 29 + 42 = 71%; democratic debate 32 + 40 = 72% (the summary on p. 5 prints 71%, rounding discrepancy not explained). Poll from January 2022, before the 2024 Olympics law and the AI Act. Percentages of the total, non-responses included (~1%). Pages cited = printed numbers (PDF page minus 1).
chf-12.population: 2,016 people representative of French people aged 18 and over, quota method (sex, age, socio-professional category, region, size of urban area), online
chf-12.question_tr: In your opinion, today, is it an absolute priority, important but not a priority, secondary or pointless… ? [item] To strengthen the legal framework that applies to the use of biometric technologies in order to better guarantee respect for people's rights (in %)
chf-12.auteur: Défenseur des droits (Defender of Rights, France), « Perception du développement des technologies biométriques en France : entre manque d’information et demande d’encadrement »
chf-12.unite: % judging it important (37) or a top priority (47) to strengthen the legal framework

chf-13.libelle_court: complaints received by the CNIL in 2025
chf-13.phrase: In 2025, the CNIL received 20,150 complaints (2025 annual report).
chf-13.limite: All categories combined, nothing on a specific sector (surveillance, biometrics, AI). Measures neither actual violations nor their severity; an increase may come from better awareness of the remedy.

chf-13.question_tr: Not applicable: activity figure. Printed labels « plaintes reçues », « plaintes traitées ».

chf-14.libelle_court: fines imposed by the CNIL in 2025
chf-14.phrase: In 2025, the CNIL imposed 83 sanctions totaling €486,839,500 in fines (2025 annual report).
chf-14.limite: Total amount dominated by two cookie sanctions (« Deux sanctions en matière de cookies expliquent l’essentiel de ce chiffre »), compared with €55,212,400 in 2024. The 83 sanctions include 78 fines, 3 liquidations of periodic penalty payments and 2 reminders of legal obligations. Nothing on a specific sector.

chf-14.unite: euros in fines in 2025; 83 penalties; 143 formal notices; 323 inspections

chf-15.libelle_court: Europeans agreeing that robots and AI require careful management
chf-15.phrase: In Special Eurobarometer 554 (April-May 2024, 26,415 people in the EU), 84% of respondents agreed that robots and AI are technologies that require careful management.
chf-15.limite: Declared opinion; a survey on AI and work, but the item is not about work alone (a neighboring item concerns use 'outside the workplace'). Value for France not read here. The "more than six in ten ... a good thing for society" of the introduction is the neighboring item 'a good thing for society, because they help people do their jobs or carry out daily tasks at home': 63%, -5 points since 2017.
chf-15.population: Residents of the 27 member states, interviewed in their mother tongue
chf-15.terrain: April 25, 2024 to May 22, 2024 (p. 7; 'FIELDWORK: April May 2024' on the cover)
chf-15.auteur: European Commission (DG EMPL), Special Eurobarometer 554, « Artificial Intelligence and the future of work », conducted by Verian
chf-15.unite: % agree (51% strongly agree) that robots and AI need careful management; -4 points since March 2017

chf-16.libelle_court: US adults more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI
chf-16.phrase: In a Pew survey from August 2024, 51% of US adults said that the increased use of AI in daily life made them more concerned than excited, compared with 15% of the AI experts surveyed.
chf-16.limite: Two US populations, not France. The expert sample is representative only of the experts who responded (p. 2). Declared opinion.
chf-16.population: 5,410 US adults (ATP panel, weighted); 1,013 experts residing in the United States (authors or presenters at 21 AI conferences in 2023 or 2024), unweighted, representative only of those who responded
chf-16.terrain: adults August 12, 2024 to August 18, 2024; experts August 14, 2024 to October 31, 2024
chf-16.unite: % of US adults 'more concerned than excited' (versus 15% of experts); 11% of adults and 47% of experts 'more excited than concerned'; 38% 'equally concerned and excited' in both groups

w12-01.phrase: The IPCC (AR6 Synthesis Report, 2023) estimates that global surface temperature was 1.09 °C above 1850-1900 on average over 2011-2020.
w12-01.limite: A ten-year average, so it lags behind recent years (see “Warming, year 2025 (WMO)” and “Warming, 2023-2025 (Copernicus)”). This is not an extinction risk. The latest IPCC synthesis report read here; whether an AR7 exists was not checked. The Paris Agreement thresholds concern the long term: this figure is not a crossing of them.
w12-01.question_tr: Difference between the global mean surface temperature, 2011-2020 average, and 1850-1900.

seuils: Pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 °C
jauge.note: max = the highest threshold cited in Article 2 (2 °C); this is a display bound chosen by us, the source gives no scale, and a value can exceed it. The thresholds concern the long term, not a single year or decade.

w12-02.phrase: The World Meteorological Organization estimates that 2025 was about 1.43 °C above the 1850-1900 average, 2025 being the second or third warmest year on record.
w12-02.limite: A single year; the WMO consolidates several datasets (Copernicus ERA5 gives 1.47 °C, see “Warming, 2023-2025 (Copernicus)”). Uncertainty of ± 0.13 °C, read in the WMO one-page fact sheet, not in the text of the web page. This is not an extinction risk. The Paris Agreement thresholds concern the long term: this figure is not a crossing of them.
w12-02.question_tr: Difference between the 2025 global mean temperature and 1850-1900, consolidation of several datasets.

seuils: Pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 °C
jauge.note: max = the highest threshold cited in Article 2 (2 °C); this is a display bound chosen by us, the source gives no scale, and a value can exceed it. The thresholds concern the long term, not a single year or decade.

w12-03.phrase: According to the Copernicus service, using the ERA5 dataset, the global average from 2023 to 2025 exceeds 1.5 °C above an estimate of the pre-industrial level (1850-1900): 1.52 °C, a first over three years in the instrumental period.
w12-03.limite: A three-year average does not match the Paris Agreement definition, which concerns the long term: the report specifies that 2025 alone is at 1.47 °C and that the current level of warming is about 1.4 °C. The JRA-3Q dataset gives 1.50 °C. This is not an extinction risk. Comparison thresholds: those of the Paris Agreement.
w12-03.question_tr: Average of 2023, 2024 and 2025 relative to an estimate of the 1850-1900 pre-industrial level, ERA5 reanalysis.

seuils: Pursue efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 °C

w12-05.phrase: In 2019, IPBES estimated that about one million animal and plant species were threatened with extinction.
w12-05.limite: A 2019 estimate, not a count: the press release writes "around 1 million" in the text and "up to 1 million" in its key figures, out of about 8 million estimated species. The IUCN Red List counts fewer threatened species because it covers only assessed species (a comparison made by us). This is not a risk of human extinction. Gauge: 1 million out of 8 million species estimated by IPBES (same page), so about 12.5% (calculated by us), order of magnitude only.
w12-05.question_tr: Number of animal and plant species that the IPBES global assessment considers threatened with extinction.

jauge.unite: millions of animal and plant species (threatened, "up to 1 million"; total estimated by IPBES: 8 million)
jauge.note: The denominator is an IPBES estimate, read on the same page, not a count; the numerator is given as "around" or "up to" 1 million. 1/8 = 12.5% is an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

w12-05.auteur: IPBES, press release of the Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
w12-05.unite: animal and plant species threatened with extinction (order of magnitude)

w12-06.phrase: The IUCN Red List (update of July 9, 2026) counts 175,909 assessed species, of which 49,505 are threatened with extinction.
w12-06.limite: 49,505 / 175,909 = 28% (calculated by us) is the share of ASSESSED species that are threatened. The gauge maximum is the number of assessed species, not the number of all species on Earth. This is not a risk of human extinction.
w12-06.question_tr: Number of species assessed by the IUCN Red List and number of species threatened with extinction according to the same update.

jauge.unite: threatened species out of species assessed by the IUCN Red List
jauge.note: max = the assessed species, not all species on Earth.

w12-06.auteur: IUCN, press release of July 9, 2026 (Red List update)
w12-06.unite: species threatened with extinction out of species assessed

w12-07.phrase: The Living Planet Report 2026 (WWF, ZSL index) gives an average decline of 73% in the size of monitored vertebrate populations between 1970 and 2022.
w12-07.limite: This is neither 73% of animals lost, nor 73% of populations or species: it is an average of relative changes in monitored populations, with 1970 as the baseline (WWF specifies this: the index measures neither the number of animals lost nor the number of populations lost). About half of the populations in the index are stable or increasing. Successive editions are not directly comparable (different species, longer period). This is not an extinction risk. Criticisms of the method in the literature were not checked here.
w12-07.question_tr: Average change in the relative abundance of 35,803 population time series of 5,790 vertebrate species, between 1970 and 2022.

jauge.unite: % average decline of the monitored population index, 1970-2022
jauge.note: An average decline of an index of monitored populations, expressed as a percentage: not 73% of animals, nor of populations, nor of species (WWF).

w12-07.auteur: WWF, Living Planet Report 2026 (index produced by ZSL)
w12-07.unite: % average decline in the size of monitored vertebrate populations, 1970-2022

w12-08.phrase: SIPRI estimates the global inventory at 12,187 nuclear warheads in January 2026, of which about 9,745 are in military stockpiles.
w12-08.limite: An estimate, not an official count. The difference (12,187 − 9,745 = 2,442, calculated by us) corresponds exactly to the "Retired" column of table 8A.1: warheads retired from service and not yet dismantled. The total number is still falling, solely because of Russian and US dismantlement (SIPRI). Says nothing about an extinction or about the use of these weapons.
w12-08.question_tr: Estimate of the total number of nuclear warheads of the nine nuclear-armed states, in January 2026.
w12-08.unite: nuclear warheads worldwide, total inventory, January 2026

w12-09.phrase: SIPRI estimates that 4,012 warheads were deployed with missiles and aircraft in January 2026, about 100 more than a year earlier.
w12-09.limite: An estimate. SIPRI puts between 2,100 and 2,200 of these warheads on high operational alert on ballistic missiles. Measures neither an extinction risk nor the chance that they will be used. Gauge: 4,012 out of 12,187 (total inventory, which includes 2,442 retired warheads), i.e. 32.9%; 41.2% of military stockpiles (9,745). Our calculations.
w12-09.question_tr: Number of warheads in military stockpiles deployed with missiles and aircraft, the rest being in central storage.

jauge.unite: deployed warheads out of total inventory, January 2026
jauge.note: Same table 8A.1 as “Nuclear warheads (SIPRI)”. The 12,187 total includes 2,442 warheads retired from service: 4,012 / 12,187 = 32.9%; for military stockpiles alone, 4,012 / 9,745 = 41.2% (our calculations).

w12-09.unite: warheads deployed with missiles and aircraft, January 2026

w12-10.phrase: On January 27, 2026, the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists set the Doomsday Clock at 85 seconds to midnight, the closest to midnight since its creation.
w12-10.limite: A committee's symbolic judgment, neither a measurement nor a numerical forecast. The Bulletin links it to nuclear weapons, climate, biology and AI. A later setting is not ruled out: the page read on November 14, 2026 still showed 85 s. This is not a measured extinction risk.
w12-10.question_tr: Setting of the clock by the Science and Security Board of the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists.

w12-11.phrase: The Planetary Health Check 2026 indicates that seven of the nine planetary boundaries are crossed.
w12-11.limite: The boundaries are reference thresholds defined by researchers ("scientifically defined guardrails" according to the page), not established tipping points; the page speaks of a risk of irreversible damage beyond them. The count depends on the assessment of each boundary, whose criterion is not detailed on the page read. This is not an extinction risk.
w12-11.question_tr: Number of planetary boundaries whose assessment indicates that they are crossed.

jauge.note: The denominator 9 is read on the page ("7 out of 9 Planetary Boundaries are breached").

w12-11.auteur: Planetary Health Check 2026 (PBScience project, Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research)
